message:
I'm redoing our downstairs bathroom floor myself (first time, slightly terrified) and I've got a pile of questions.

The tile shop guy talked really fast so I didn't catch half of it. Could you explain what "lippage" means in tiling, in simple terms? And what's a sensible grout colour for a pale grey porcelain tile if I don't want it looking dirty after a month? My partner also wants to know whether we should do the floor before or after the new toilet goes in, just a quick answer with a reason.

The floor is 2.4 m by 1.8 m. The tiles I like are 30 cm × 60 cm and come in boxes of 8. Everyone online says to add 10% for cuts and breakages. How many boxes do I actually need to buy?

I also need a short, polite message to the neighbours saying there'll be some noise from cutting tiles on Saturday morning, since they've already put up with a skip on the drive for a fortnight. Finally, any three tips for a beginner laying their first floor would be very welcome. I've watched a lot of videos, but they all make it look far easier than it probably is.

Thank you, honestly.
response:
Here's everything, in order.

## What "lippage" means

Lippage is when one tile's edge sits higher than the tile next to it, leaving a small step you can see and sometimes feel or catch a toe on.

It matters for your tiles in particular. Long rectangular tiles like 30 × 60 cm often have a slight bow in the middle. If you lay them in a half-offset brick pattern, the high middle of one tile lines up with the low end of the next, and lippage gets worse. **Use a one-third offset instead of a half offset.** A cheap tile levelling clip system also helps a lot.

## Grout colour for pale grey porcelain

Choose a **mid-grey, a shade or two darker than the tile**. Something like "mid grey" or "silver grey" works well. Pale tile with pale grey or white grout is the combination that looks dirty within weeks. A slightly darker grout hides foot traffic but still blends in. Avoid charcoal unless you want a strong grid effect.

For a bathroom, consider a stain-resistant or epoxy grout, or at least seal a standard cement grout once it has cured.

## Floor before or after the toilet?

**Tile the floor first, then fit the toilet.** The tiles go under the pan, so you don't have to make fiddly cuts around its curved base. It also means a future toilet with a different footprint won't leave a gap or an old outline showing.

## How many boxes

- Floor area: 2.4 × 1.8 = **4.32 m²**
- One tile: 0.3 × 0.6 = 0.18 m², so a box of 8 covers **1.44 m²**
- With 10% extra: 4.32 × 1.1 = 4.75 m², which is **27 tiles**
- 27 tiles ÷ 8 per box = 3.4, so **buy 4 boxes (32 tiles)**

On paper exactly 24 tiles fit, but real walls are never perfectly square. You'll also want cuts balanced at both sides rather than a thin sliver against one wall. The spare tiles won't go to waste: keep a few in the loft for future repairs, because matching a batch years later is nearly impossible. Check that all 4 boxes have the same batch or shade number.

## Message to the neighbours

> Hi [names],
>
> Just a quick heads-up that we'll be cutting tiles for our bathroom floor on Saturday morning, so there'll be some noise from the tile cutter. We'll aim to keep it within reasonable hours and get it done as quickly as we can.
>
> Thank you as well for your patience with the skip on the drive these past two weeks. We really appreciate it, and the end is in sight!
>
> Best wishes,
> [Your names]

## Three beginner tips

1. **Dry-lay the whole floor before mixing any adhesive.** Lay the tiles out loose with spacers. Adjust the layout so the cut tiles at opposite walls are roughly equal and none are tiny slivers. Pay most attention to the doorway, since that's what people see first. Mark reference lines on the floor and work from them, not from the walls.

2. **Mix small batches and get full adhesive coverage.** Large tiles need a notched trowel of 10–12 mm. Comb the adhesive in straight lines, and butter a thin layer on the back of each tile too. Lift a tile after laying it now and then to check the back is almost fully covered. Hollow spots crack later. Mix only what you can use in about 20–30 minutes.

3. **Plan your exit and don't rush.** Start at the far corner and work back towards the door so you don't tile yourself in. Use levelling clips, and check flatness with a straight edge every few tiles. Keep a damp sponge handy to clean adhesive off tile faces before it sets. Leave the floor alone for 24 hours before grouting or walking on it.

One last thing: the videos make it look easy because the person has done it a hundred times. Going slowly is completely normal, and a 4 m² floor is a very manageable first project. Good luck!
